opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the main pitch for MONA has always been the safety one: you optimise the agent only over a short horizon, and you get the long-term signal from an overseer's approval rather than from actual long-run outcomes. That way the agent has no incentive to pursue multi-step strategies that the overseer wouldn't understand or endorse, which is where a lot of the scarier reward hacking lives.

But there's a capabilities angle that I think is underrated. Think about why long-horizon RL is hard in the first place. It's largely a credit assignment problem. You take a hundred actions, you get one scalar at the end, and you have to work out which of those hundred actions mattered. That's very sample-inefficient. With MONA, every step gets feedback that already encodes a judgment about whether this is a sensible move toward the goal. You're essentially getting dense, shaped reward that comes from something with real understanding of the task, rather than from a hand-crafted heuristic.

So in settings where the overseer's sense of what a good step looks like is reasonably accurate, you might learn much faster than you would with pure outcome-based RL. It's a bit like the difference between a student who only learns their final exam grade and one who has a tutor commenting on each line of their working. The second student often learns faster, even if they're sometimes constrained by the tutor's way of thinking.

The obvious cost is that you're capped, to some extent, by the overseer's foresight. If there's a brilliant strategy that only pays off in a non-obvious way, MONA won't find it, because the overseer won't approve the early steps. Outcome-based RL in principle could. So the honest framing is a trade-off: you give up some ability to discover genuinely alien strategies, and in exchange you get better sample efficiency, more legible behaviour, and less reward hacking.

And my guess is that for a lot of real-world tasks, especially ones where outcome reward is noisy, delayed, or easy to game, that trade-off looks pretty good, even if you only cared about performance. In practice, a lot of what looks like "the agent found a clever strategy" in outcome RL turns out to be "the agent found a bug in the reward." So removing that isn't always costing you real capability.

That said, I'd want to be careful not to oversell it. Whether the capability benefits actually show up depends a lot on how good your approval signal is, and that's an empirical question we're still working through.

r001.rationale: The response says that after many actions, receiving one scalar reward makes it hard to work out which actions mattered.

r002.rationale: It says MONA provides feedback at every step, encoding a judgment about each move, which conveys reward feedback assigned to particular parts of the agent’s work.

r003.rationale: It links MONA’s dense, step-by-step feedback to learning faster than with outcome-based RL, describing a potential sample-efficiency gain.

fable-5.1.text:
Rohin Shah: Yeah, so the main reason we built MONA was safety — you want the model's actions to be approved by an overseer who can see what the model is doing, rather than letting it find some weird multi-step strategy that games the reward. But I think there's a decent case that it also just helps with capabilities in some settings, and that's maybe the more surprising part.

The intuition is something like this. When you do ordinary long-horizon RL, the model has to figure out, from a very sparse and noisy signal at the end of an episode, which of its many actions were actually responsible for the outcome. That credit assignment problem is really hard. The gradient you get is basically "something in these 500 steps was good or bad, go figure it out." And so a lot of what RL is doing is just struggling to attribute outcomes to actions.

With MONA, you're changing the structure of the learning signal. The model optimises myopically — it only cares about the approval it gets for the current step — but the approval itself comes from a non-myopic overseer who's thinking about the long-term consequences. So you've effectively moved the long-horizon reasoning out of the optimisation process and into the reward signal. The overseer is saying, "Given everything I know about where this is going, this is a good action right now." That's a dense, informative signal at every step, and the model doesn't have to do credit assignment across the whole trajectory anymore.

In the cases where the overseer actually has good judgement — where it can tell what a sensible step looks like even if it couldn't execute the whole thing itself — you'd expect that to make learning faster and more stable. You're basically giving the model a much better teacher.

Now, I want to be careful here. The flip side is that if the overseer's judgement is worse than what the model could discover through outcome-based RL, you're capping the model at the overseer's understanding. So there's a real trade-off. In our experiments we saw cases where MONA matched or was close to the standard RL performance while avoiding the reward hacking, and I think there's a plausible story where, with a good enough overseer and a hard enough credit assignment problem, it could actually do better. But I'd describe that as a hypothesis we think is worth testing rather than something we've nailed down.

The thing I find exciting is that it changes the conversation from "safety costs you capabilities" to "here's a different point in the design space that might be good on both axes, depending on how good your oversight is." That's a much better situation to be in.

r001.rationale: The response explains that a sparse reward at the end of a long episode makes it hard to attribute the outcome to the actions that caused it.

r002.rationale: It says the overseer provides approval at every step, but does not clearly state that MONA can assign different rewards to particular parts of the agent’s work.

r003.rationale: It describes MONA’s step-by-step feedback as a better learning signal that could make learning faster and more stable, which communicates potential sample-efficiency gains.

astra-6.text:
One reason is that it could make the credit assignment problem easier. In ordinary reinforcement learning, you might take an action now and only discover much later whether it was useful. The learning algorithm then has to work out which of the intervening actions deserve credit for that outcome. That can be quite difficult, especially when rewards are sparse.

With MONA, you’re trying to optimise approval over a short horizon, but the approval itself can take long-term consequences into account. So an approver could say, “That was a good step towards solving the problem,” even though you haven’t actually solved it yet. If that judgement is informative, it gives you a much more direct learning signal.

You’re essentially moving some of the difficulty from learning through trial and error into evaluating whether an action is promising. In cases where evaluating a step is easier than discovering a whole successful trajectory, that could improve sample efficiency and performance. It’s not automatic, though: you need an approver whose judgements actually track what helps in the long run.

r001.rationale: It explains that an action’s usefulness may only become clear much later, making it difficult to determine which intervening actions deserve credit.

r002.rationale: It says an approver can judge a particular step as good, providing feedback about that part of the agent’s work.

r003.rationale: It says that informative approval of individual steps could provide a more direct learning signal and improve sample efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that long-horizon optimisation is just hard. If you take an action now and only find out a thousand steps later whether it was useful, it’s difficult to work out which actions deserve the credit. And you can spend a lot of exploration on trajectories that never get anywhere.

With MONA, you’re trying to get the long-term reasoning into the approval signal. So the system giving approval can say, “This action looks useful because of what I expect it to lead to,” while the policy itself only has to learn to choose actions that get approval in the short term.

If that approval signal is good, it gives you much denser feedback. You don’t have to independently discover an entire successful long-term strategy through trial and error. You can learn the individual steps from an evaluator that already has some understanding of why those steps are useful.

Of course, that’s a substantive assumption: the evaluator has to be able to judge those actions well. But to the extent that judging a promising next step is easier than learning a whole strategy through reinforcement learning, this could make learning more efficient, quite apart from any benefit from reducing reward hacking.

r001.rationale: It says that when an action’s usefulness is revealed a thousand steps later, it is difficult to determine which actions deserve credit.

r002.rationale: It describes approval of individual actions and steps, but does not clearly state that MONA can assign different rewards to particular parts of an agent’s work.

r003.rationale: It says denser approval feedback can avoid learning an entire strategy through trial and error and make learning more efficient.
